<reason>A razor-thin-to-clear PRO win. CON was the sharper, more vivid debater (Tom Cruise dubbing, Hepburn's voice, "only the star gets the padlock," "launders them") and landed real pressure on materiality vagueness and the boilerplate-consent problem. But CON's route to victory was eroded by its own moves: it conceded collective bargaining should reach digital replicas (conceding the motion's substance and quarreling only about forum, while importing a "statutory" framing the motion never specified), and it conceded cloning a refused line is a real wrong, leaving it to argue that contract law already covers it. PRO's reply—that an actor should not have to anticipate and prohibit every future alteration, and that silence is not consent—kept the default framing on PRO's side. PRO answered both pressure questions directly with a workable reasonable-viewer standard that excluded CON's jawline/syllable hypotheticals, and its closing met the boilerplate argument head-on ("less protection, not more"; upfront authorization is how the right is acquired, not proof of failure). CON's second horn (studios avoiding weaker performers) was thin, and two clipped rebuttals cost it the tail of its nonunion argument. PRO was less memorable but made the decision easier: material synthetic performances require asking and paying, ordinary editing is untouched.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The refused-line exchange: PRO's Q1 forced CON to concede cloning a refused line is a real wrong; CON's A1 cleverly narrowed it to a contract-law case already handled, but PRO's closing turned that back—if the actor must expressly refuse every future alteration to be protected, CON has made the studio's default entitlement the rule, which is exactly what the motion contests.</best_rebuttal>
